newsitem.title: MEXICO: TV mogul's death robs Mexico govt of key ally.
newsitem.headline: TV mogul's death robs Mexico govt of key ally.

text.p: Facing key mid-term elections and a growing opposition challenge, Mexico's government has lost a staunch ally with the death of powerful TV tycoon Emilio Azcarraga, analysts said on Thursday.

The influence of Azcarraga's giant Televisa Group on Mexico is hard to exaggerate. Juan Molinar, a political scientist, likened it to "the equivalent in the U.S. of putting ABC, NBC and CBS all together."
Televisa's precursor, XEW Radio, was founded by Azcarraga's father Emilio Azcarraga Vidaurreta in 1930 -- the year after the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) was formed.
The two have worked hand in hand ever since, commentators say, with the PRI ruling Mexico and the Azcarragas the airwaves.

"This is one of the classic empires built on political connections," said Federico Esteves, a professor at the ITAM university in Mexico City. "Azcarraga is one of the last of a dying breed here who built empires in political cahoots with the ruling class."
Successive PRI presidents always counted on Televisa for support, enjoying favourable coverage and watching the political opposition ignored or ridiculed.
Alan Riding, in his 1984 book on Mexico "Distant Neighbours," likened Televisa to "the country's Ministry of Culture, its Ministry of Education and its Ministry of Information."
Azcarraga himself was never ashamed of his support for the government of the day. Riding quoted him as once having said his "only boss is the President of the Republic."
Political scientists say Televisa has opened up a little since then, allowing the opposition some space and being less obvious in its support for the government.
Cable and satellite competitors have entered the fray, offering more diverse coverage and allowing Mexicans a glimpse of other news programmes, such as those on America's CNN.
Most importantly for Televisa, former president Carlos Salinas de Gortari broke the company's domestic monopoly by privatising a state-run station as a competitor.
The new rival, TV Azteca, has "begun to oblige Televisa to change to reflect the changing market," Esteves said -- though he added that Azteca is also generally pro-government.
But at crucial moments, Televisa still delivers the goods for the PRI, which faces key congressional and gubernatorial elections in July.
When President Ernesto Zedillo earlier this week wanted to reply to opposition attacks on him for appearing at a party event to push PRI candidates, his aides spoke to Televisa.

The result was a 10-minute pre-recorded Zedillo television address inserted into "24 Hours," Televisa's prime news programme. No balancing opposition comment was included, and anchor Jacobo Zabludovsky told viewers after the address ended: "I think the message is clear."
The Televisa empire is now in the hands of Azcarraga Milmo's son, Emilio Azcarraga Jean.

At 29, Jean lacks his father's clout and presence. He indicated in a recent interview with the Mexican news magazine Proceso that he was more interested in making money from entertainment programming -- a traditional Televisa strength -- than in slanting news coverage.
"I am not a politician and moreover I don't understand politics," he told Proceso.
Nevertheless, most commentators believe Televisa will maintain its cosy relationship with the Mexican government.

"If they stopped supporting the PRI, they would lose their concessions faster than you can say Mass," joked Rafael Segovia, an academic at the Colegio de Mexico. "The government can't do without them and they can't do without the government."
